title: How to read a cross-stitch chart
subtitle: The grid, the key, the centre, and where the first stitch goes
excerpt: A cross-stitch chart is a grid where one square is one stitch. This is how to read one: the key and its symbols, the centre marks, counting in tens, the back-stitch layer, part-filled squares, joining printed pages, and how the same chart looks on screen.
sourceNotes: Chart-reading conventions are shared across counted cross-stitch traditions. The grid-and-key format is documented in the Priscilla needlework books (1900s) via the Internet Archive, and Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, covers the charted method in the cross-stitch chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cross-stitch worked from a gridded chart by counting squares rather than following a printed design on the fabric. The stitcher counts the Aida squares against the chart squares to place each stitch correctly. This method gives precise, repeatable results on any fabric count.
The list printed beside a cross-stitch chart that pairs every symbol or colour in the grid with a thread code and colour name. Nothing appears in the grid that is missing from the key.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.
The number of stitches per inch of fabric. A 14ct fabric gives 14 stitches per inch; 18ct gives 18. A higher count makes the finished piece smaller and the stitches finer.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.

A stitch that fills part of a fabric square instead of all of it. A quarter stitch runs from one corner into the centre of the square; a three-quarter stitch is a half stitch plus a quarter. Charts use them on curves and points.

content.text: A cross-stitch chart is a map of the finished piece drawn on a grid. One square on the grid is one stitch on your fabric. The square tells you which thread colour to use, and the list beside the chart says what every mark in the grid means.
Counted cross-stitch
works this way because nothing is printed on the cloth. You count squares across and down from a known point, and that count puts each stitch where it belongs.
What you need

items.name: The chart, printed on paper or open on screen
Aida fabric, 14-count, cut larger than the design
Stranded cotton in every colour the key lists
A highlighter, a ruler or a magnetic strip for keeping your place on a paper chart

content.text: The parts of a chart
The grid.
Each small square is one full cross. Heavier lines divide the grid into blocks of ten squares so you can count in tens instead of one at a time.
The key.
The
chart key
runs down the side or along the bottom. Each row pairs one symbol or colour with a
floss
code, and usually a colour name. Nothing appears in the grid that is missing from the key.
The centre marks.
Small arrows or a short line on the margins mark the middle row and the middle column. Where the two meet is the centre of the design.
Symbols or colour blocks.
Some charts print a symbol in each square. Some print the square filled with the thread colour. Many print a symbol inside a coloured square.
Back-stitch lines.
Thin lines drawn along the edges of the squares rather than inside them. They are a separate layer, worked on top of the finished crosses.
Part-filled squares.
A square split by a diagonal, or holding a small triangle, asks for a stitch that fills part of the square rather than all of it.
Working through a chart
Find the centre marks on the chart and follow them in until they meet. Ring that square in pencil.
Fold your fabric in half, then in half again. Where the two creases cross is the centre of the
Aida
, and it matches the square you have just ringed.
Count out from the centre of the chart to the first stitch you mean to make, using the heavy lines to count in tens.
Count the same number of squares out on the fabric and bring the needle up in that hole. One chart square is one fabric square, whatever the
fabric count
Stitch one colour at a time inside a block of ten squares by ten squares, then move to the next block.

Check the finished block against the chart before you start the next one. When the shape on the fabric matches the shape on the chart square for square, and the heavy lines land on the stitches you counted, the block is right.
Work the back-stitch lines last, once every cross around them is finished.
Counting in tens

The heavy lines every ten squares are the most useful thing on the chart. Count the blocks first, then the loose squares inside the last block. Nine blocks and three squares is ninety-three stitches, counted in two goes instead of ninety-three. A single miscounted square is easy to make and hard to spot; a whole block out of place shows up at once against the heavy lines.
Symbols or colour blocks

Symbols are easier to tell apart. Two close shades of green look almost the same as blocks of colour, but a triangle and a circle never do. Colour blocks are easier to read at a glance, because the picture is already there in front of you. If one version of a chart is hard to follow, look for the other version of the same design before deciding it is beyond you.
Back-stitch lines
A
back-stitch

line is drawn along the edges of the squares. It carries the outlines, the whiskers, the lettering and the stems, and it is what makes a design look drawn rather than blocky. Work it after the crosses in that area are done, or the line sits underneath them and vanishes. The key lists back-stitch colours in their own section, and they are usually worked in one strand where the crosses take two.
Part squares and fractional stitches
A
fractional stitch

fills part of a square instead of all of it. A square split by a diagonal with one half shaded asks for a three-quarter stitch in that colour. A square split between two colours or two symbols asks for a three-quarter in one and a quarter in the other. Charts use them on curves and points, where a full square would look stepped. The short leg goes into the middle of the Aida square, so the needle passes through the woven block rather than into a hole.
Charts that run over several pages

A large chart will not fit on one sheet. Printed charts are split across pages, and the pages overlap by a row or two so nothing is lost at the join. The overlap is usually shaded, or marked along the edge with a row of small arrows. Line the pages up on that shaded strip rather than on the cut edge of the paper, or the design gains a row every time you cross a join. Number the pages before you cut anything, and keep the small page map that shows how they fit together.
Reading the same chart on screen

The Studio shows a chart three ways and the switch sits above the grid. Colour blocks look like a printed colour chart. Stitched crosses draw each square as the cross it will become, which is closest to the finished fabric. Symbols only shows the same black and white symbols a printed chart uses, so it prints cleanly and reads square for square against a paper chart. All three sit on one grid with the same heavy lines every ten squares, so a count made in one view holds in the others. Marking squares off as you stitch keeps your place, which is the job a highlighter does on paper.
Common mistakes

attrs.heading: What goes wrong
attrs.intro: The five that catch most people out.

items.symptom: The design ends up off-centre, with no room on one side
items.cause: Counting started from a corner of the chart instead of the centre.
items.fix: Start at the centre of the chart and the centre of the fabric and work outward. The margins then come out even on all four sides.

items.symptom: A whole section sits one row out from the rest
items.cause: One square was miscounted early in a row and the error carried along it.
items.fix: Count in blocks of ten against the heavy lines rather than square by square, and check each block against the chart before moving on.

items.symptom: Two colours in the finished piece look the same
items.cause: The chart was read as colour blocks and two close shades were mixed up.
items.fix: Switch to the symbol view, or find the symbol version of the printed chart. Symbols separate shades that colour does not.

items.symptom: The outlines disappear into the stitching
items.cause: Back-stitch was worked before the crosses around it.
items.fix: Finish every cross in the area first, then lay the back-stitch on top.

items.symptom: The design gains a row where two printed pages meet
items.cause: The pages were joined on the cut edge instead of the overlap.
items.fix: Find the shaded overlap strip on each page and line the pages up on that, so the repeated rows sit on top of one another.

content.text: When you use this

Every counted design is worked this way, from a motif that takes an evening to a sampler that takes months. The same reading applies to a chart in a magazine, a chart you have downloaded, and a chart open in the Studio. Blackwork and needlepoint charts use the same grid and the same kind of key, so a chart you can read here you can read there.
The
cross-stitch stitch guide
lists every stitch a chart can ask for, with its symbol and a reminder of how it is worked.
